Pure text retrieval has the opposite weakness: it may fetch passages that sound close to the question but do not preserve the graph route that proves the answer. Multi-hop answering also has a compounding-error problem. If the first retrieved fact points in the wrong direction, later steps can become confident elaborations of a bad start. The abstract adds another tension: the system must be token-efficient, so it cannot simply paste every candidate path into the language model. It must choose. But choosing too aggressively risks dropping the one path that connects the needed facts. The paper is about balancing path coverage, semantic fit, verification, and repeated correction when the model signals uncertainty.
548.naive: A smart beginner would first ask for the shortest graph path between entities mentioned in the question, then hand that path to the language model. If several paths are available, the beginner might take the top few by length or by keyword overlap. This fails because length is only a crude cost. A short path may connect the right entities through an unhelpful relation, and a text-heavy match may ignore the graph's direction and relation types. Another beginner solution is one-shot retrieval: fetch once, generate once, and stop. That fails when the model's first evidence set is missing an intermediate fact. The system needs a way to search several plausible paths, score them by meaning as well as topology, filter weak ones, and revise the search when uncertainty appears.
548.ap: The core idea is to treat graph evidence as candidate paths that must earn their place before the language model sees them. S-Path-RAG first searches for bounded-length paths, so the route cannot grow without control. It gives path choices weights that include semantic fit, meaning how well the path's entities and relations match the question's intended meaning. It combines several search habits: k-shortest path search to find multiple cheap routes, beam search to keep only promising partial routes as they grow, and constrained random walks to sample alternatives without wandering anywhere. Then it learns a path scorer, a path encoder trained to separate useful paths from less useful ones, and a lightweight verifier. Instead of dumping full path text into the model, it injects a compact soft mixture of selected path representations, while keeping interpretable path traces for diagnosis.
548.mech: The mechanism begins with a question and a large knowledge graph. The system identifies graph seeds, which are starting entities or nearby graph regions tied to the question. From those seeds it enumerates candidate paths with a length bound, because multi-hop reasoning needs several links but cannot afford an unlimited walk. The hybrid search then keeps a diverse set of plausible routes: weighted k-shortest search favors low-cost paths, beam search keeps the best partial candidates at each expansion step, and constrained random walking adds controlled exploration so the system is not trapped by one early scoring mistake. Each candidate path is represented by its entities, relation labels, and semantic match to the question. A learned scorer assigns usefulness to paths. A contrastive path encoder, meaning a component trained by comparing good paths against poorer alternatives, learns to place question-supporting paths closer to the question signal than distracting paths. A lightweight verifier filters or checks selected paths before they influence generation. The chosen paths are not merely pasted as long text. They are compressed into a soft mixture of path latents, meaning compact internal summaries of several selected routes with different weights. Cross-attention, the model operation that lets the answer generator consult those summaries while writing, injects this graph evidence. If the language model emits concise diagnostic messages showing uncertainty, the Neural-Socratic Graph Dialogue loop maps those messages to targeted graph edits or seed expansions, then retrieval adapts and runs again.
548.math: Several mathematical ideas are working together. The first is path search on a graph. A graph is a set of points and links; a path is an ordered walk through links. Shortest-path math turns route choice into a cost problem: assign costs to links or paths, then find low-cost routes. Here the cost is not just distance. Semantic weighting adds a meaning score so that a relation path matching the question is preferred over a merely short route. Beam search is a budgeting idea: while building paths step by step, keep a small frontier of promising partial routes and discard the rest, trading completeness for speed. Constrained random walks add controlled sampling, letting the system explore nearby alternatives while respecting bounds. The learned path scorer is an ordering function: it maps a candidate route to a number so routes can be ranked. The contrastive encoder uses comparison as its teacher: pull useful question-path pairs closer in representation, push less useful ones apart. The verifier adds a second check, reducing blind trust in the scorer. The soft mixture is weighted averaging over selected path summaries, preserving several pieces of evidence without spending full text length. Cross-attention is weighted consulting: while generating each part of the answer, the model chooses which path summaries matter most.
548.dots: This paper connects directly to the conference's recurring problem of evidence selection under uncertainty. In the retrieval-augmented answer family, the shared failure is that outside evidence helps only if the system chooses the right evidence and notices when retrieval is incomplete or conflicting. S-Path-RAG gives that problem a graph shape: the witnesses are not isolated documents but relation paths. It also sits in the knowledge-graph family, where repo metadata describes sibling systems such as RPO-RAG, GCA-KBQA, HyperRAG, and unified graph answer systems as different ways to make relation paths ground generated answers. Compared with ordinary ranking papers, this one ranks paths rather than products or documents. Compared with graph-learning papers, it does not only spread evidence through neighbors; it searches, scores, verifies, and feeds selected routes to a language model. The same ideas touch similarity, ranking, graph reasoning, and efficiency: measure meaning, order candidates, follow links, and save scarce input length.
548.ww: It should work better than the naive approach because it respects two facts at the same time. First, a multi-hop answer depends on structure: the order of relations matters, not just whether related words appeared in some retrieved text. Enumerating graph paths preserves that chain. Second, structure alone is not enough: the shortest or most connected route can still be irrelevant. Semantic weights and learned scoring let the system prefer paths that fit the question's meaning. The verifier adds a safeguard against a path scorer that is confidently wrong. The compact mixture helps because the language model receives concentrated graph evidence instead of a bulky list of path descriptions, reducing the chance that important support is buried. The iterative dialogue loop helps when the first retrieval round is incomplete. If the model's diagnostic message indicates uncertainty, the retriever can expand seeds or edit the graph search target rather than forcing an answer from weak evidence. The improvement comes from coordinated search, ranking, compression, and feedback, not from any single named component.
548.po: The claimed payoff is a question-answering system that is more accurate, covers the needed evidence better, and runs more efficiently end to end than strong graph-based and language-model-based baselines. The abstract says the system is token-efficient and topology-aware, which means it tries to spend the model's limited input space on compact graph paths that preserve relation structure. It also preserves interpretable path-level traces, so errors are easier to diagnose and interventions are more concrete: a person can inspect which route influenced the answer instead of only reading the final generated text. The ablations and diagnostic analyses are meant to show how semantic weighting, verifier filtering, and iterative updates trade off against one another.
548.limits: The abstract supports the design but leaves important assumptions. The method needs the knowledge graph to contain enough of the right entities, relations, and paths; if the crucial fact is missing, stale, mislabeled, or poisoned, path search may only make the wrong evidence look orderly. Semantic weighting assumes the system can judge meaning well enough to compare candidate paths, and the verifier assumes weak paths have detectable signs. Bounded search can miss longer but necessary routes, while random exploration can still waste effort. The soft mixture may save input length but can hide details that a full path text would expose. The reported benchmark gains do not prove reliability across all graph domains, adversarial graphs, or questions whose answer requires evidence outside the graph.

549.bp: The real object in this paper is control over an increasingly independent language system. A large language model can now answer users, call tools, draft plans, help moderate content, and sometimes take steps with little moment-by-moment human direction. Once a system acts in that kind of setting, a basic governance question appears: who or what notices when it is drifting away from the rules, and who has authority to correct it? The paper asks whether the model itself can play that role. It does not treat self-governance as a vague claim that the model is smart enough to behave well. It defines the idea operationally: the system would need to watch its own behavior, regulate itself when needed, and keep its behavior aligned with internal values. The paper's deeper concern is that operational control is not the same as moral responsibility, so self-checking machinery cannot replace human-centered governance.
549.wh: The hard part is that governance has two different meanings that are easy to confuse. One meaning is mechanical: a system notices a forbidden answer, compares its behavior with a constraint, and changes course. A language model can partly do that if it has feedback loops, built-in constraints, or training that helps it adjust its own behavior. The other meaning is normative: a system understands why a value matters, owns the responsibility for following it, and can be held accountable when it fails. The abstract argues that language models do not have that second capacity. They can process rules and produce rule-shaped behavior, but the values come from training, prompts, design choices, and institutions outside the model. The tension is therefore not simply whether the model can detect an error. It is whether detection and correction are enough to count as governing itself when accountability, moral agency, and value grounding remain external.
549.naive: A smart beginner might say: give the model a constitution, ask it to inspect its own answers, and let it refuse or rewrite anything that violates the rules. That is attractive because it keeps governance inside the same system that produces the behavior. But the paper's abstract points to the failure: checking a rule is not the same as being the source of the rule or being answerable for its consequences. The model may monitor and regulate outputs, yet it still depends on externally supplied values and externally designed consequences. If those values conflict, are incomplete, or are gamed by a situation the designers did not expect, self-review can produce a polished answer without true accountability.
549.ap: The paper's core idea is to split self-governance into parts instead of treating it as an all-or-nothing property. It proposes an operational definition built from self-monitoring, self-regulation, and internal value alignment. Self-monitoring means the system has some way to inspect its own outputs or internal state for signs of trouble. Self-regulation means it can change behavior after that inspection, such as stopping, revising, refusing, or routing a case differently. Internal value alignment means the model's behavior is shaped toward stated values from within the system's learned or architectural machinery. The paper then evaluates mechanisms that can support these partial abilities: feedback loops inside the architecture, constraints embedded into the system, and meta-learning, where the system learns how to adjust across tasks. Its central move is careful boundary drawing: these mechanisms can produce operational self-regulation, but not full normative self-governance.
549.mech: The mechanism in the paper is an analytic pipeline rather than a new deployed model. The input is the practical fact named in the abstract: large language models are being deployed in more autonomous roles, so governance must cover behavior that may unfold without direct human steering at every step. First, the paper defines what would have to be present for self-governance to be meaningful in operational terms. It separates three moving parts: a monitoring part that detects whether the model's behavior needs review, a regulation part that changes behavior in response, and an alignment part that keeps those changes pointed toward values rather than arbitrary output preferences. Second, it examines architectural supports for those parts. Internal feedback loops let the system compare a proposed answer or action with some signal about acceptability, then revise. Embedded constraints place boundaries inside the generation process, so some behaviors are discouraged or blocked before release. Meta-learning adds an adaptation layer: the system uses previous tasks or feedback to improve how it adjusts in new cases. Third, the paper compares this machinery with the stronger demand of normative governance. The output is a distinction: language models can implement partial self-regulation, but the authority, value source, and accountability structure still need human-centered governance around the model.
549.math: The main mathematical ideas are feedback control, constraint satisfaction, learning from repeated correction, and alignment as a comparison between behavior and desired values. Feedback control starts with a simple loop: observe what the system is doing, compare it with a target condition, and adjust the next action to reduce the mismatch. In this paper, the target is not temperature or speed but acceptable model behavior. Constraint satisfaction means treating some rules as boundaries on possible outputs or actions. The system does not merely ask which answer is likely; it must also ask whether the answer fits restrictions that designers placed around safety, control, or policy. Meta-learning is learning how to learn: instead of only storing one behavior, the system learns patterns for adapting when a new situation or correction appears. Alignment is a scoring problem in plain terms: behavior is judged by how well it matches values supplied by people or institutions. The tradeoff is autonomy versus accountability. More internal correction can make the model faster and less dependent on humans for routine failures, but the math only compares behavior with supplied signals. It cannot by itself create moral agency or decide who is responsible when the value signal is wrong.
549.dots: This paper connects to the conference's broader language-model and agent work because it asks what must surround a fluent model before it can be trusted as a worker. Tool-use and agent papers study how a model chooses actions, calls outside systems, and manages long tasks; this paper studies the control question that appears once those actions matter. It also connects to misinformation, trust, and audit work, where the recurring problem is that a convincing output is not enough. There must be a way to inspect evidence, identify responsibility, and decide whether confidence is deserved. The abstract's emphasis on embedded constraints and feedback loops also neighbors safety and evaluation papers that place gates around model behavior. Its distinctive role is philosophical and governance-oriented: it says internal checks may be useful, but they remain complements to external oversight because values and accountability are social and institutional objects, not just model behaviors.
549.ww: The distinction works because it matches the layered nature of real governance. At the lowest layer, a model can plausibly catch some of its own failures. If an output conflicts with a supplied rule, a feedback loop can make the model revise it. If a constraint is embedded in the system, certain answers can be blocked or reshaped before the user sees them. If the model has learned from many correction episodes, it may become better at spotting situations that require caution. Those are real forms of operational control, and they are stronger than simply hoping the first answer is acceptable. But the same reasoning shows why full self-governance does not follow. The model's rule, target, and correction signal still come from outside design choices. It has no independent standing as a moral agent, no grounded ownership of the values it follows, and no final responsibility when a decision harms someone. The paper therefore improves the naive view by separating useful internal machinery from the larger human question of legitimate control.
549.po: The payoff is conceptual clarity for building and regulating autonomous language-model systems. Instead of answering yes or no to whether large language models can govern themselves, the paper gives a more useful split. They can perform some operational self-regulation through monitoring, constraints, feedback, and adaptation. They cannot, according to the abstract, provide full normative self-governance because moral agency, value grounding, and accountability remain unresolved. That helps designers avoid two mistakes: dismissing all internal safeguards as meaningless, or treating internal safeguards as a substitute for human-centered governance. The result is a governance vocabulary that supports layered control.
549.limits: The abstract presents a technical, ethical, and philosophical analysis, not an empirical demonstration that a specific architecture governs itself in deployment. It names mechanisms such as feedback loops, embedded constraints, and meta-learning, but it does not specify experiments, failure rates, or formal tests for deciding when self-monitoring is adequate. The argument assumes a meaningful difference between operational self-regulation and normative self-governance, and its conclusion depends on the claim that current language models lack moral agency, value grounding, and accountability. It also does not settle how human-centered governance should be designed, who should hold authority, or how conflicts among human values should be resolved.

550.bp: People use stickers as small acts of conversation. A sticker can soften a refusal, show embarrassment, signal teasing, or say "I understand" without spelling it out. A retrieval system for stickers therefore has a different job from ordinary image search. It is not only finding a picture that contains a cat, face, or gesture. It is trying to match a user's communicative need with a visual expression. The paper studies this matching problem under a realistic source of failure: users keep inventing new ways to ask, and sticker collections keep adding new visual styles. A phrase the system has never seen may still mean a familiar feeling, and a new sticker may express that feeling with unfamiliar art. The paper proposes XAlign-SR to make sticker search depend less on memorized query-sticker pairs and more on the abstract intent shared by the words and the image.
550.wh: The hard part is that the thing being retrieved is not a literal object. If a user types "that was awkward," the right sticker may show a sweating cartoon face, a nervous animal, or a character hiding behind a wall. The query and the sticker live in different forms: one is language and one is visual expression. Even worse, the bridge between them is cultural and personal. Different users describe the same intent in different words, and different artists draw the same intent in different visual styles. The abstract names this as an out-of-distribution problem, meaning the system is tested on queries and stickers that do not look like the examples it learned from. A retriever that mostly remembers common phrase-picture pairings can look good on familiar cases but return irrelevant or inappropriate stickers when either side is new. The central tension is surface match versus intended meaning.
550.naive: A smart beginner might build two simple lookup systems. First, label each sticker with a few words, then match the user's query to those labels. Second, train a text-image matcher on examples of successful query-sticker pairs and rank stickers by the learned score. Both can work when the test case resembles past data. They fail when expression moves outside the seen patterns. A new sticker may not have the expected label words, and a new query may express the same mood through slang, understatement, or context. The model may also overvalue obvious visual cues, such as a smile or tears, even when the communicative intent is sarcasm, hesitation, or playful disagreement. The failure is not lack of search machinery; it is using the wrong level of meaning.
550.ap: The paper's central move is to align abstract expressive intent across the two forms. In plain terms, it tries to make the system ask: what conversational act is this query trying to perform, and what conversational act does this sticker visually perform? XAlign-SR is motivated by symbolic interactionism in cognition, which the abstract invokes as the idea that meaning is not only inside a word or picture by itself; it is formed through shared social symbols and interactions. For sticker retrieval, that means the useful common object is intent, not raw text or raw pixels. The method therefore aims to place a query and a sticker near each other when they carry the same expressive purpose, even if their wording or art style is unfamiliar. The constructed OOD benchmarks then test whether that intent-level bridge holds under unseen queries and unseen stickers.
550.mech: The mechanism begins with a user's query and a collection of candidate stickers. The query provides words that hint at a communicative need: joking, consoling, refusing, celebrating, reacting with confusion, or another expressive act. Each sticker provides visual evidence: facial expression, pose, symbols, scene, style, and other cues that may stand for an intent. A basic retrieval model would compare query and sticker directly and rank candidates by surface compatibility. XAlign-SR adds an intermediate target: abstract expressive intent. The query side must be transformed from wording into a description of what the user wants to convey. The sticker side must be transformed from visual appearance into the same kind of intent description. The two transformed descriptions are then aligned, meaning the system is trained so matching intents from the two sides become easier to compare, while mismatched intents are separated. At retrieval time, the system scores candidate stickers by how well their inferred intent lines up with the query's inferred intent, and returns the highest-scoring stickers. The paper also builds evaluation settings from sticker datasets that simulate realistic query-sticker cases outside the familiar training pattern. Those tests matter because the claimed improvement is not just better matching on remembered examples, but stronger behavior when new queries or new stickers appear.
550.math: The main mathematical idea is similarity under a chosen meaning. Similarity is not automatic; the system must decide which differences matter. For this paper, two stickers can be visually different but similar in intent, and two smiling stickers can be different if one is sincere and the other is teasing. The method therefore needs a shared comparison space, a numeric map where text-derived intent and image-derived intent can be compared. The word "alignment" means training that map so paired or compatible query-sticker meanings move closer together, while incompatible meanings move farther apart. This is a compression tradeoff. Rich language and rich images are squeezed into shorter internal descriptions, so the system must preserve the parts that matter for conversational purpose and let go of decorative details. Retrieval then becomes ranking: every candidate sticker receives a score for how well it fits the query's inferred intent, and the top items are shown. The out-of-distribution part adds a generalization requirement. The learned map should not merely memorize known pairs; it should capture stable social symbols that repeat across new phrasing and new visual designs. The mathematical risk is false closeness: if the map treats superficial emotion cues as intent, it can confidently retrieve the wrong sticker.
550.dots: This paper sits inside the repository's multimodal retrieval and broader multimodal vision-language family because it asks unlike evidence to cooperate before a decision is made. It is close to the similarity concept: the system must define what "near" means when one object is a text query and the other is an expressive image. It is also close to ranking, because the practical output is an ordered list of stickers from a large collection, and a small error near the top directly changes the user's conversation. Its out-of-distribution emphasis connects it to other 2026 papers about systems that fail when tomorrow's inputs differ from yesterday's examples, including graph, recommendation, and generative AI robustness work in the repo. The shared field-level problem is brittleness under change. Here the change is not a new class label or a new graph pattern; it is new human expression across language and visual culture.
550.ww: The approach should help when communicative intent is more stable than surface form. Many phrases can mean embarrassment, and many drawings can depict embarrassment, even when the exact words and exact art are new. If training teaches the retriever to attend to that shared intent, then an unseen query does not have to match a known phrase, and an unseen sticker does not have to duplicate a known visual template. The system can succeed by recognizing that both sides point to the same social use. This is stronger than direct phrase-label matching because it gives the model a middle layer of explanation: the query and sticker agree because they perform the same expressive function. It is stronger than generic image-text matching because sticker relevance often depends on what the image is used to say, not simply what it depicts. The OOD benchmarks are important because they test the exact promise: separating reusable intent from accidental training patterns.
550.po: The payoff is a sticker retrieval system that is less likely to return irrelevant or inappropriate stickers when users write unfamiliar queries or when the sticker set contains unfamiliar visual designs. Grounded in the abstract, XAlign-SR is reported to significantly outperform existing baselines on constructed out-of-distribution benchmarks that simulate realistic query-sticker scenarios. In practical terms, the system buys better matching between what a user wants to express and what a sticker communicates. That matters for chat products because a wrong sticker is not just a search miss; it can change the tone of a conversation. The method also gives platforms a path toward handling new sticker packs and changing user expression habits.
550.limits: The claim depends on the constructed OOD benchmarks reflecting real sticker use. If the benchmarks miss cultural differences, private chat context, sarcasm, group-specific slang, or rapidly changing meme conventions, the measured robustness may overstate deployment reliability. The method also assumes that abstract expressive intent can be inferred from a query and a sticker without full conversation context. That may fail when the same sticker is playful in one thread and rude in another. Alignment can hide details: two items may look close in intent while differing in appropriateness, audience, or cultural meaning. The abstract reports significant outperformance but does not specify costs, latency, failure categories, or whether the method remains reliable across languages and communities.

551.bp: Large language models now help write, answer, recommend, summarize, and sometimes steer decisions on the Web. That means their behavior is no longer just a question of whether an answer is fluent; it is also a question of which human values the answer respects. The hard part is that values are plural. One person may want maximum helpfulness, another may want caution around harm, another may prize honesty even when the answer is uncomfortable. VC-Soup serves the practical problem of building one model behavior that can balance several such values without training a new model for every possible mixture. The paper treats alignment as a data and model-combination problem: first find preference examples where the values mostly point in the same direction, then train models on that cleaner ground, then combine the resulting model settings to reach balanced trade-offs.
551.wh: The difficulty comes from two pressures meeting at once. First, a real deployment cannot afford a separate large model for every value recipe. If there are many values and many possible weights on those values, the number of custom models grows quickly. Second, the values can disagree on the same example. A response that is useful may be less cautious; a response that avoids risk may be less direct. If the training data mixes these conflicts without noticing them, the model receives opposing signals about what a better answer is. Existing routes named in the abstract, including reward reweighting, prompt-based supervised fine-tuning, and model merging, try to adjust value emphasis after or during training. The paper says they still suffer when conflict is strong: the model may not learn a smooth behavioral direction for each value, so later combinations damage alignment instead of blending it.
551.naive: A smart beginner might score every candidate answer on each value, choose weights for the values, add the scores together, and train one model to prefer the answer with the highest weighted total. For another community, change the weights and train again. That is understandable because it turns many values into one number. It fails in two ways described by the paper. Repeating this for each value mixture is expensive because each mixture can require its own policy model. More importantly, adding scores hides conflict. If one value strongly prefers answer A while another strongly prefers answer B, the total score may force a compromise example that teaches neither value cleanly.
551.ap: VC-Soup's core move is to ask whether each preference example is internally cooperative before using it. For a pair of possible model answers, the method looks at the reward gap for each value: how much that value prefers one answer over the other. It then compares the whole list of gaps with an all-ones direction, meaning the direction where the values agree rather than pull against one another. Examples with low cross-value coherence are filtered out. The remaining preference pairs are used to train policy models whose behavior changes smoothly for the value they are meant to represent. Because those models were trained on less contradictory evidence, their model settings are more likely to sit on compatible paths. The method can then linearly combine the policies and keep combinations that are not plainly worse for the values being balanced.
551.mech: The mechanism starts with value datasets made of preference pairs. Each pair contains two possible model responses, and each value has a reward signal saying which response it likes more, or by how much. For each pair, VC-Soup forms a reward-gap vector: a small list whose entries are the value-by-value differences between the two responses. If most entries point the same way, the pair is value-consistent: it says, in effect, that many values agree about which response is better. If the entries point in different directions, the pair contains a conflict. The paper measures this by cosine similarity, which compares the direction of that gap list with the all-ones vector. A high score means the list points toward shared agreement; a low score means the values are not moving together. The method filters out low-consistency pairs inside each value dataset. It trains policy models on the remaining data, aiming for smoother value-consistent behavior and better linear mode connectivity, which means two trained models can be connected by straight-line mixtures of their settings without passing through badly performing behavior. Finally, it forms linear combinations of these policies and applies Pareto filtering, keeping balanced choices where improving one value would require giving up another.
551.math: The main mathematical object is a vector, which here is simply an ordered list of numbers, one number per value. For a preference pair, each number records a reward gap: how much that value favors one answer over the other. The important question is not only how large the gaps are, but whether they point in the same direction. Cosine similarity answers that by comparing directions rather than raw size. If the reward-gap list points close to the all-ones list, the values are broadly saying the same thing. If it points away, the example asks the model to serve incompatible goals at once. The second idea is filtering as controlled forgetting: discard examples whose signal would teach conflict more than shared structure. The third idea is linear combination of parameters, where a model's learned settings are treated like coordinates and blended by weighted averaging. This only makes sense if the trained models lie in compatible regions, so the paper uses value-consistent data to preserve linear mode connectivity. Pareto filtering adds a trade-off test: keep solutions where no value can be improved without making another value worse.
551.dots: This paper sits with other WWW work on large language models and trust, especially the neighboring self-governance paper in the same batch. Both ask how model behavior can be constrained by values rather than judged only by answer quality. Their emphasis differs: self-governance asks whether a model can regulate itself and where human accountability remains necessary, while VC-Soup asks how to produce model policies that balance several measured values. It also connects to recommendation and ranking papers because it is ultimately sorting possible behaviors under competing goals. A value score is like a preference signal: it tells the system which answer should rank higher for one purpose. The paper's filtering move resembles broader conference ideas about removing noisy or misleading evidence before learning from examples. Its model-combination step connects to efficiency work because it seeks many value trade-offs without retraining every separate model from scratch.
551.ww: The method should help because it separates two problems that are easy to confuse. Some preference examples teach broad alignment because many values agree: an answer may be more honest, safer, and more helpful all at once. Other examples mostly teach a collision between values. If a model trains heavily on collisions, its learned settings may encode sharp compromises that do not combine well with settings from another value model. VC-Soup keeps the examples that reveal shared structure first. That gives each policy model a cleaner path: it can learn what its value means on cases where the signal is not being constantly contradicted. Once the policies are smoother and more compatible, averaging their settings is less likely to produce a model that falls between behaviors in a broken way. Pareto filtering then protects the last step by rejecting combinations that are dominated, meaning another available combination is at least as good on every value and better on one.
551.po: The payoff is a cheaper and more controllable route to multi-value alignment. Instead of training a fresh large model for every desired value mixture, VC-Soup trains value-consistent policies and combines them. The abstract reports extensive experiments and theoretical analysis showing that this mitigates value conflicts and consistently outperforms existing multi-value alignment methods. Practically, that means a deployed model could be tuned toward balanced behavior across diverse human values with less wasteful retraining and less damage from contradictory preference data. The gain is not just a higher score; it is the ability to search the trade-off surface among values more directly.
551.limits: The paper depends on reward signals that meaningfully represent the values being balanced. If those rewards are shallow, biased, or missing important human context, the value-consistency score can only organize flawed evidence. Filtering also has a cost: examples with real moral tension may be removed, even though deployment often needs models to handle exactly those hard cases. Linear merging assumes the trained policy models remain compatible enough that averaging their settings gives useful behavior. Pareto filtering can identify balanced candidates among measured values, but it cannot prove that unmeasured values, rare harms, or future user communities are protected. The abstract reports experiments and theory, but it does not specify all value definitions or deployment conditions.

552.bp: The ordinary object here is a changing network: people contact other people, devices send messages, accounts trade with accounts, or financial instruments start moving together. At one moment two points in the network are separate; later a link appears. Dynamic link prediction asks which links are likely to appear next. That matters because a social platform may want to anticipate new interactions, a communication system may need to prepare capacity, and a financial model may watch for relationships that are forming before they are obvious. The paper's setting is not a fixed graph, like a map printed on paper. It is a graph with history. The same pair of nodes may look unimportant at one time and likely to connect later because of recent activity, slower repeated cycles, or broader temporal pressure. TFWaveFormer is built for this setting: predicting future links when the signal lives both in network structure and in how that structure changes over time.
552.wh: The hard part is that network change does not happen at one speed. Some links are driven by quick bursts: a message reply, a short communication spike, or a sudden market movement. Other links are driven by slower rhythms: habits, weekly cycles, long-term social drift, or gradual financial coupling. A model that looks only at the next timestamp can miss the slow pattern. A model that smooths everything into one long trend can wash out the short burst. Transformer-based temporal graph methods help because they can compare many moments and relationships, but the abstract says their performance is still limited when the temporal dynamics are complex and multi-scale. The tension is therefore between local detail and broad temporal dependence. The model needs to notice sharp nearby changes without losing the long-range story, and it needs to do this while the object being predicted is a graph, where links depend on both time and relationships among nodes.
552.naive: A smart beginner might store the graph at each time step, look at recent link patterns, and predict that pairs with many recent interactions, shared neighbors, or repeated past links are the pairs most likely to connect next. This can work for simple cases because recent behavior often carries useful evidence. It fails when recent evidence is only one layer of the story. A pair may connect because of a slow periodic pattern even if the last few steps look quiet. Another pair may show a sudden spike that matters briefly but should not be confused with a lasting trend. Treating all time changes as one ordinary sequence forces fast, medium, and slow signals into the same channel, so the model either overreacts to noise or ignores meaningful short events.
552.ap: The core idea is to make the model listen to the graph's history at several temporal speeds at once. TFWaveFormer combines temporal-frequency analysis with wavelet decomposition. In plain terms, it breaks a changing signal into pieces that describe different kinds of motion: quick wiggles, medium-scale changes, and slower background movement. Instead of using a traditional wavelet transform as a fixed repeated procedure, the paper proposes a learnable multi-resolution module built with parallel convolutions. That means the model can adapt how it extracts patterns at different scales from the training data. It then uses a hybrid Transformer module to bring two views together: local wavelet features that capture nearby multi-scale changes, and global temporal dependencies that compare broader parts of the history. The central move is not simply adding another model layer. It is separating temporal evidence by scale before fusing it back for link prediction.
552.mech: The input is a dynamic graph: a sequence of graph snapshots or temporal link observations from which the system must decide which node pairs are likely to form links in the future. First, TFWaveFormer builds temporal representations, which are machine-readable descriptions of how the graph has changed over time. It also builds spectral representations, meaning descriptions of the same history in terms of frequencies, or how rapidly patterns rise, fall, and repeat. The temporal-frequency coordination mechanism makes these two descriptions work together rather than treating time order and frequency content as unrelated evidence. Next, the learnable multi-resolution wavelet decomposition module separates the temporal signal into several scales. The abstract says this is done through parallel convolutions, so several filters inspect the history at the same time, each suited to a different temporal width. This replaces the traditional iterative wavelet process with a version whose filters can be learned. Those extracted pieces become local wavelet features: small-scale descriptions of changes at different speeds. Finally, the hybrid Transformer module fuses these local features with global temporal dependencies. A Transformer is a learned comparison machine: it decides which past moments or derived features should influence the current prediction. The output is a score or decision for future links, evaluated by whether the predicted links match later graph observations.
552.math: The mathematical ideas are graph prediction, decomposition by scale, frequency analysis, learned filtering, and weighted comparison. A graph is a set of nodes plus links; link prediction asks for a score on possible future links. Because the links change over time, the model is also handling a sequence. Frequency analysis is the idea that a changing signal can be described not only by when values occur, but by how fast patterns repeat or fluctuate. Wavelets refine that idea by keeping time location and scale together: they can describe a short burst without pretending it lasts forever, and they can describe a slower trend without treating every small wiggle as equally important. Multi-resolution means looking with several window sizes, like using both a close-up lens and a wider lens on the same history. Convolutions are sliding filters that repeatedly check local patterns; here they are parallel so different scales can be extracted at once. The Transformer part performs weighted comparison, assigning more influence to the moments and features that help predict a candidate link. The central tradeoff is detail versus stability: keep fast local changes, but also preserve slow structure and global temporal context.
552.dots: This paper belongs to temporal graph learning, where the repeated problem is that relationships are not static facts; they are events unfolding over time. It connects to graph reasoning because the thing being predicted is a future edge between nodes, and neighboring structure can carry evidence about that edge. It connects to sequence modeling because the past order of graph changes matters: the same links in a different order may imply a different future. It also connects to similarity and compression ideas in the repo's current math data, which describes this paper as keeping the few dimensions that matter and measuring nearness in a useful space. TFWaveFormer's particular branch is multi-scale temporal modeling. Neighboring papers may use attention, recurrence, point-process assumptions, or graph smoothing, but the shared pressure is the same: real systems change at mixed speeds, and a single flat history representation is too blunt for future-link decisions.
552.ww: The mechanism should help because it matches a real property of dynamic networks: the causes of future links often operate at different temporal scales. If a communication pair tends to reconnect after short bursts, a fast-scale feature can carry that clue. If a financial relationship appears through slower co-movement, a low-frequency feature can preserve it. If a social tie is influenced by both recent interaction and longer group activity, the fused representation can use both. The wavelet part reduces confusion by separating quick changes from slow background movement before the model decides what matters. The learnable version is important because the useful scales may differ across datasets and applications; fixed hand-designed filters might cut the history at the wrong widths. The Transformer part then adds selective comparison across the extracted features and past moments, so the model is not forced to average everything. Compared with the naive recent-history strategy, this gives the predictor separate places to store bursts, rhythms, and long-range dependencies.
552.po: The payoff is better future-link prediction in changing graphs. The abstract reports extensive experiments on benchmark datasets and says TFWaveFormer outperforms existing Transformer-based and hybrid models across multiple metrics. In practical terms, the claimed capability is earlier and more accurate anticipation of new relationships in social network analysis, communication forecasting, and financial modeling. The paper also offers a modeling lesson: temporal-frequency analysis and wavelet decomposition can be useful not only for ordinary time series, but for graph histories where the target is a future connection between nodes.
552.limits: The abstract supports the architecture and reported benchmark gains, but it does not give enough detail to prove why every component is necessary in every setting. The method assumes that future links are partly explained by multi-scale temporal patterns visible in past graph data. If links are driven by outside shocks, missing node information, policy changes, or adversarial behavior not present in the history, the wavelet and Transformer machinery may confidently model the wrong signal. The abstract also does not specify computational cost, data requirements, interpretability, or whether the learned scales transfer across domains. Strong benchmark performance is evidence of usefulness, not proof that all dynamic networks share the same temporal-frequency structure.

553.bp: Social platforms are not used in one uniform way. One person may mostly scroll, another may like and repost, and another may publish original posts that other people react to. Those differences matter because a platform is both a place where people act and a machine that decides what they see next. This paper studies that ordinary object: the everyday activity stream of X users over time. The need comes from a gap in how online participation is usually measured. If researchers ask people how they use social media, the answer can be vague, flattering, forgetful, or too coarse to show session-by-session habits. The paper instead uses high-resolution logs from 209 U.S. X users over four weeks. It asks whether actual behavior separates users into meaningful profiles, and whether those profiles are tied to demographics, ideology, content exposure, and the likely uneven effects of platform governance.
553.wh: The hard part is that social-media use is continuous, mixed, and partly invisible to the user. A person can spend a long session reading without leaving public traces, or can make a few visible posts that look more important than hours of silent viewing. Likes, reposts, posts, views, and sessions are different kinds of actions, so counting only one kind gives a distorted picture. The political and informational side is also hard because content exposure is not only a matter of declared preference. It is shaped by what the user does, what the platform shows, and what other people produce. A survey cannot easily recover that fine structure. Even logs do not speak for themselves: they must be grouped in a way that separates stable behavioral patterns from random daily variation. The central tension is turning many small traces into profiles without pretending every user fits a stereotype perfectly.
553.naive: A smart beginner might count each user's posts, likes, or total time and then place people into simple bins such as low, medium, and high activity. That would be easy to explain, but it would confuse different forms of participation. A person who reads a lot but rarely clicks might be treated as inactive, even though the platform is still shaping their information environment. A person who posts little but likes and reposts often may have a different role from a person who publishes original content. Another naive move is to trust self-reports, but people may not remember scrolling sessions accurately and may describe their public identity rather than their actual behavior. The paper needs a grouping method that uses many session-level signs together.
553.ap: The core idea is to let behavior patterns define the user types rather than forcing users into categories chosen in advance. The paper uses session-level activity features from four weeks of X logs and applies latent profile analysis. A latent profile is a hidden group inferred from visible measurements: the group label is not directly observed, but it explains why several measured behaviors tend to appear together. The resulting profiles are interpretable in ordinary language. Lurkers, the largest group, mainly consume content with less visible action. Interactors participate through actions such as liking or reposting. Creators, the smallest group, publish more. The paper then connects those profiles to demographics and content exposure, finding that interactors and lurkers skew younger and Democratic, while creators skew older and more Republican and consume more ideological and low-credibility content.
553.mech: The mechanism starts with raw user activity logs rather than retrospective survey answers. For each of the 209 U.S. participants, the study observes four weeks of behavior on X at the level of sessions. A session is a bounded period of use, so the unit of evidence is not only whether the person ever posted, but how their viewing, scrolling, liking, reposting, and posting behavior appears across repeated visits. Those session-level features become the measurements for each user. The next step is grouping. Latent profile analysis looks for several recurring behavioral mixtures that can explain the observed measurements. Instead of giving every user a single hand-written score, it asks whether the data is better described by a small number of hidden profiles, each with its own typical pattern. Each user is then associated with one of the discovered profiles. The output groups are lurkers at 60.45 percent, interactors at 32.52 percent, and creators at 7.03 percent. After that, the study compares the groups on outside and downstream properties: engagement intensity, demographics, ideology, and the kinds of content they encounter. The final product is not a recommender or moderation rule. It is a behavioral segmentation showing that participation style is linked to systematically different information environments.
553.math: The main mathematical idea is probabilistic grouping from repeated measurements. Probability is useful here because the paper is not observing a clean label called lurker, interactor, or creator in the logs. It observes many noisy signs, then estimates which hidden profile best explains their joint pattern. The word hidden matters: a profile is an inferred cause-like summary of visible behavior, not a field recorded by the platform. Latent profile analysis treats each user as likely to have been generated from one of several behavior mixtures. Each mixture has expected levels of session features, and users are assigned according to which mixture makes their observed actions most plausible. This is different from a fixed threshold because the boundary is learned from how behaviors co-occur. The study also uses comparison: once groups are formed, it compares their demographics and content exposure. The mathematical tradeoff is compression versus detail. Compressing many sessions into three profiles makes the platform easier to reason about, but it loses individual nuance. The method fits because the problem is about finding repeated shapes in messy activity, while keeping uncertainty visible enough to avoid claiming that every person in a profile behaves identically.
553.dots: This paper sits in the repo's User behavior theme and connects strongly to Social Networks and Influence. Many neighboring papers study ranking, recommendation, moderation, misinformation, or platform governance after a system has decided what to show. This one looks one step earlier: users differ in the behavioral channels through which ranking and exposure can affect them. It connects to the information concept because silent viewing is information-rich even when it leaves few public signals; logs reveal behavior that visible posts alone would hide. It connects to probability because the profiles are inferred from repeated cases rather than directly observed labels. It also touches moderation and governance work because interventions may land differently across groups. A rule aimed at creators, a feed change aimed at lurkers, or a friction added to reposting can alter different parts of the participation system. The broader lesson is that platform effects are filtered through user roles, not merely through content categories.
553.ww: The approach should work better than the naive version because it respects the multi-part nature of participation. If a researcher measures only posting, creators dominate the story and lurkers disappear. If the researcher measures only time spent, quiet consumption and active engagement can look too similar. By using session-level logs, the paper can see both visible and quiet behavior across repeated use. By grouping several behavioral signs together, it can detect that a user type is a pattern, not a single action count. That matters for ideology and content exposure because the platform experience is produced through repeated small interactions. A creator's feed, audience, and incentives may differ from a lurker's, and an interactor's likes and reposts may steer future exposure differently from silent scrolling. The profiles therefore create a clearer comparison: not just who says they use X, but which role they appear to play in the platform's attention system. This makes uneven effects of governance easier to notice.
553.po: The payoff is a more grounded map of online participation. The paper reports three behavior profiles in the studied group: lurkers are most common, interactors are a substantial minority, and creators are rare. It also links these profiles to engagement intensity, demographics, ideology, and content exposure, including the finding that creators consume more ideological and low-credibility content. For platform researchers, this buys a way to study users who are active as viewers even when they are publicly quiet. For policy and moderation work, it warns that the same intervention may not reach, burden, or protect all user types equally.
553.limits: The abstract supports careful behavioral segmentation, not a universal typology of all X users. The sample is 209 U.S. users tracked for four weeks, so the profiles may change with country, platform design, election timing, news cycles, or longer observation windows. The analysis assumes the logged session features capture the important parts of use and that latent profile analysis finds meaningful groups rather than convenient summaries. The labels lurker, interactor, and creator simplify people who may move between roles. The abstract reports links with ideology and low-credibility exposure, but it does not prove whether behavior causes exposure, exposure changes behavior, or both are shaped by another factor.

554.bp: Online platforms are not only places where people post; they are places where people decide who may enter their field of view. Moderation usually sounds like a central authority removing harmful posts or accounts, but Bluesky also lets users and communities block accounts and share blocklists. That creates a different kind of moderation system: many small decisions, made by users rather than the platform alone, combine into a large visibility filter. This paper asks what that system looks like when it can finally be measured. Because Bluesky makes moderation actions public by design, the authors can study blocking across 34 million users, including direct individual blocks and blocks routed through blocklists. The practical question is whether community moderation merely gives users local control, or whether it becomes an infrastructure that shapes most content visibility on the platform.
554.wh: The hard part is that blocking is both a personal choice and a network event. One user blocking another may mean harassment avoidance, political disagreement, spam control, community boundary-setting, or simple dislike. A blocklist adds another layer: one person's judgment can be reused by many others, so a local decision can become a shared moderation rule. On most platforms, researchers cannot see enough of this process because moderation and blocking data are private. Without that evidence, it is easy to overstate either side: community moderation may be celebrated as user empowerment or dismissed as fragmentation without measuring how widely it acts. Bluesky changes the evidence problem, but the interpretation remains difficult. The same public blocking record must be mapped as volume, structure, correlated account traits, and downstream consequences, while avoiding the mistake of treating correlation as proof that blocking caused every later change.
554.naive: A smart beginner would count how many accounts were blocked and maybe compare that number with official takedowns. That would show whether user blocking is common, but it would miss the system. Blocking matters through who blocks whom, whether blocklists amplify particular judgments, what traits blocked accounts tend to have, and whether being blocked changes later visibility, popularity, activity, or social links. Another beginner move would be to label blocked accounts as simply harmful. That also fails. The abstract says blocked accounts are often active, popular, toxic, and politically inclined, and that different blocklists target different account types and behaviors. A single moral label would erase this variety.
554.ap: The paper's central move is to treat public blocking records as a measurable moderation ecosystem rather than as isolated user preferences. It first maps the blocking actions at platform scale, separating individual blocks from blocklist-mediated blocks. It then asks what signals travel with being blocked: activity, popularity, toxicity, political inclination, and the differences among blocklists. Finally, it checks consequences instead of stopping at description. If blocking is meant to reduce exposure or dampen harmful influence, then blocked users might become less visible, less active, less popular, or less central in the social graph. The authors report a mixed result: blocking is massive and affects the visibility of more than 90 percent of Bluesky content, yet it does not decrease blocked users' popularity and activity and has limited effect on the social graph. The core idea is measurement of trade-offs, not an automated moderation classifier.
554.mech: The mechanism begins with a platform where moderation actions are public by design. The inputs are records of users, individual block actions, blocklists, content visibility relationships, and account-level signals that the abstract names as activity, popularity, toxicity, and political inclination. The first step is mapping: represent users as accounts and blocking actions as directed relations, where one account or blocklist places another account behind a visibility barrier. This turns moderation into a network that can be counted and structured. The second step separates sources of blocking. A direct block is one user's decision; a block through a blocklist is a shared list being adopted or applied, so it can spread one moderation judgment across many users. The third step compares blocked and unblocked accounts on observed signals. This does not prove why each block happened, but it reveals which measurable traits are associated with being blocked. The fourth step compares blocklists with each other, because the abstract says they target different account types and behaviors. The final step measures consequences: after identifying blocked accounts and the reach of blocking, the study checks whether those accounts lose popularity or activity and whether the follower or interaction graph changes substantially. The output is a quantitative picture of scale, targets, variation, and effects.
554.math: The main mathematical object is a directed network. The nodes are Bluesky accounts, and a block is a one-way link saying that one account has chosen to limit another account's visibility. Blocklists add a group-mediated layer: a list can act like a bundle of many directed links adopted by others. Counting is the first tool, but it is not trivial counting, because the same blocked account may appear in many relations and the same content may be affected by many visibility barriers. Correlation is the second tool. The paper compares blocking status with signals such as activity, popularity, toxicity, and political inclination, asking which traits appear more often among blocked accounts. This is probability language in everyday terms: from repeated observations, estimate which features tend to travel together. The third idea is consequence measurement over a graph. If blocking reshaped the platform, one would expect measurable changes in popularity, activity, or social connections. The trade-off is local control versus global reach. A block is simple for one user, but many blocks and blocklists can create large-scale visibility changes without the same effect as centralized removal. The math fits because moderation here is not one decision; it is many linked decisions accumulating across a social network.
554.dots: This paper connects to the repo's social-networks-and-influence family because the object is a web of users whose relationships affect what information can travel. It also connects to misinformation and trust work, not because the abstract studies false claims directly, but because platform trust depends on who can see, avoid, amplify, or filter harmful and disputed content. Compared with papers that build detectors for toxic or misleading posts, this study measures a human and community control mechanism already operating in the platform. It is also close to fairness and governance papers: different blocklists targeting different account types means moderation is pluralistic, but also uneven. The neighboring user-behavior paper in the same batch studies lurkers, interactors, and creators on X; both papers show that platform-level conclusions can be wrong if users are treated as one uniform population. Here, the recurring conference idea is graph measurement under social meaning: links are actions, but their social interpretation is contested.
554.ww: The approach works better than the naive count because it respects the shape of the phenomenon. Community moderation is not only about how many blocks exist; it is about where blocks concentrate, how blocklists multiply decisions, what kinds of accounts attract blocks, and whether the resulting barriers actually change behavior or network structure. By measuring individual blocks and blocklist-based blocks separately, the study can see the difference between private avoidance and reusable community policy. By comparing blocked accounts with signals like activity, popularity, toxicity, and political inclination, it can test whether blocks are randomly scattered or aligned with visible account traits. By measuring downstream consequences, it avoids assuming that a large moderation volume automatically weakens blocked users. That last point is especially important: the abstract reports that blocking is several orders of magnitude more common than official takedowns and affects most content visibility, yet blocked users do not become less popular or less active. The method therefore turns a debate about community moderation into a set of observable tensions: reach, targeting, pluralism, and limited behavioral impact.
554.po: The payoff is empirical grounding for designing moderation systems that are not purely centralized. The paper shows that community blocking on Bluesky is not a small side feature: it is widespread, much larger in volume than official takedowns, and touches the visibility of more than 90 percent of content. It also shows that this power has mixed consequences. Blocked accounts tend to have strong signals such as high activity, popularity, toxicity, and political inclination, but blocking does not appear to reduce their popularity or activity. Designers therefore get a clearer design problem: user control can reshape exposure without necessarily solving platform-wide influence.
554.limits: The findings depend on Bluesky's unusual public-by-design moderation data, so they may not transfer to platforms where blocks are private or where blocklists work differently. The abstract reports correlations with toxicity, politics, popularity, and activity, but it does not prove why each user blocked each account. Public data can show patterns, not private intent. The consequence claims also require careful timing and measurement choices that the abstract does not fully describe. Limited effect on the social graph does not mean limited emotional or community effect for individual users. Finally, the abstract is truncated, so details about toxicity measurement, political inference, sampling, and causal controls are not visible here.
